rewrites.summary:
Belarus is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. In 2024 the authorities escalated from hostility to active persecution: a Culture Ministry decree reclassified transgender identity itself — "the desire to live and be seen by others as a person of an opposite sex" — as pornography, punishable by up to four years in prison. In September 2024 a wave of arrests targeted the community: the local organisation TG House Belarus documented over 15 LGBTQ+ people detained, including at least eight transgender people, several arrested for merely subscribing to "extremist" resources online.

Detained trans people were beaten and forced to record humiliating "confession videos" circulated on pro-government channels. The human-rights watchdog ODIHR's 2024 reporting notes the majority of bias incidents targeted trans people, including "physical assaults, threats, abductions, humiliation, and coerced confessions related to their gender identity by law enforcement officers." National media runs systematic dehumanising propaganda. A post-dating April 2026 law criminalises "propaganda of homosexual relations, gender reassignment, childlessness" — a new enforcement layer; acts remain legal, protections remain zero.

For a visitor: gender transition technically remains legal, but the 2024 decree and the 2026 law mean a discoverable online presence or simply living visibly as trans can be prosecuted. No documented trans-tourist case exists yet, but police actively hunt trans people, any visible gender nonconformity risks detention, and foreign nationals receive no protection.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Adjacent, not core: the national prosecution office has signalled an administrative-penalty law against "LGBTI propaganda" that had not yet been tabled when the 2025 review was written, and a 2024 treaty-body digest of 25 SOGIESC decisions includes jurisprudence relevant to this nation among other nations — litigation flux rather than local enforcement. A 1999 foreign-ministry report supplies an historical baseline for the government's record.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Gender transition technically remains legal for residents, but the 2024 pornography decree criminalises living visibly as trans — the decree's prosecution machinery targets residents' daily lives.

Resident data: the 2025 regional review records that at least ten trans people left the country in a year due to discrimination and repression, and accounts of the September 2024 wave note some of the detained fled the country. No cultural-gender-role or birth-register facts are recorded.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
General political repression and the post-2020 protest crackdown affect everyone; the score reflects trans-specific risk.

No documented trans-tourist case exists yet, and no source addresses border-screening or document-practice for trans visitors; the April 2026 law post-dates every cited source, so its enforcement practice is unverified. Official hate-crime statistics are unavailable — this nation has not reported to the watchdog ODIHR since 2015 and has no national point of contact — so account-level figures cannot be cross-checked.

rewrites.summary:
Ukraine is workable for trans visitors — with the caveat that this scores trans-specific risk, not the general risks of an active war zone. Nothing about being trans is criminalised; legal gender recognition exists (medicalised — a "transsexualism" diagnosis and psychiatric observation under the 2016 protocol); civil society, including two support NGOs and other groups such as Gender Stream and Insight, operates openly, and the capital Kyiv hosted a three-day Trans Forum in June 2026 even during the war.

For a visitor: a foreign passport is not subject to conscription rules, so border crossing follows standard wartime entry rules, but wartime document checks can out people, and civil-society groups report that since martial law began, holders of male gender markers were stopped at the border. There is no SOGI-specific hate-crime law, societal attitudes lag the regional average, and the healthcare system is war-disrupted (hormone shortages, diagnostic corruption reported). No marriage- or partner-travel-specific rule for visitors is documented.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Scoring context: Ukraine ranks far above its neighbours Russia (0.12) and Belarus (0.13) — no criminalisation, no state persecution — and below two other neighbours, Serbia (0.64) and Moldova (0.65), reflecting wartime institutional strain and weaker legal protections rather than active hostility. In flux: the June 2026 Trans Forum debated the new draft Civil Code's effect on the transition procedure and whether being trans grounds exemption from mobilisation.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The medicalised legal-gender-recognition protocol (a "transsexualism" diagnosis and psychiatric observation under the 2016 protocol), the martial-law exit ban on trans women with male passports, and the war-disrupted healthcare (hormone shortages, diagnostic corruption) are resident-facing.

Resident data: in 2016 a court ordered the passport and document changes requested by two trans people without requiring sterilisation; a 2012 attack on a resident activist near his home (the second in six weeks) drew no immediate police response; and the monitoring organisation Amnesty International's 2013 report described a pervasive climate of homophobia and urged lawmakers to reject criminalisation proposals.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
General war risks (missile strikes, infrastructure, mobilisation) apply to all travelers and are out of scope for the trans-specific score; trans residents' draft exposure is context, not the visitor score.

One cited news piece (June 2022) was not retrievable at research time. No source directly documents visitor border-screening practice for trans foreigners, and no marriage- or partner-travel-specific consequences for visitors are recorded.

rewrites.summary:
Moldova is workable for trans visitors — the best-protected in its immediate neighbourhood. Since 2022, anti-LGBT hate speech and hate crimes are criminal offences covering SOGI explicitly, and the equality law was amended in 2023 to cover sexual orientation and gender identity; the capital Chisinau's Pride marches through the city centre under police protection, and police have deployed tear gas against anti-LGBT protesters seeking to disrupt it.

Counterweights for a visitor: no accessible legal gender recognition exists for anyone (a medicalised process exists on paper but is reported not functional in practice); the predominant Orthodox Church and major politicians (including the capital's mayor) regularly issue homophobic statements that colour the climate; and the breakaway separatist region of Transnistria, controlled by the neighbouring power Russia, has its own anti-LGBT "propaganda" law — travelers should treat that region as a separate, much riskier jurisdiction.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Context rather than visitor-facing mechanism: Moldova is on the EU accession path, which drives continued legal alignment. Legal flux: in 2013 an appeals court struck down a local "gay propaganda" ban as unconstitutional after church-led bans and protests against the anti-discrimination law; hate speech remains serious with no meaningful state response, and election-period political hate speech has risen, per the 2024 review. A recent travel feature portrays the country as slowly emerging from its past to carve a new queer identity, with public Pride proceeding openly.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The non-functional legal-gender-recognition process is resident-facing.

Resident data: an equality-body study found acceptance of LGBT+ people extremely low — 79% would not accept LGBT+ neighbours, 60% not as work colleagues (social-distance score 5.7) — and marginalisation increased in 2022; in 2024 a trans woman was denied bank service over a document/appearance mismatch and the equality body confirmed discrimination.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The breakaway region of Transnistria is scored as part of Moldova de jure, but travelers should treat it separately: foreign-controlled, anti-LGBT "propaganda" law, no consular access. General poverty and corruption affect all travelers. No source addresses border-screening or document-practice for trans visitors, and no visitor-specific incident record exists to independently verify the assessment.

rewrites.summary:
Luxembourg is exceptionally safe — among the strongest trans jurisdictions in its region. Legal gender recognition by self-determination has existed since 2018 (Act of 10 August 2018) with no medical requirements, and notably the process is open to foreign nationals as well as citizens. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is banned across employment, goods, services, education, and health; a national LGBTI action plan has operated since 2018; an equality body handles complaints.

No traveler-facing concerns exist: no bathroom laws, no border issues (entry under the common border-free travel zone), no documented anti-trans violence pattern. Gaps are minor: no nonbinary marker, and gender expression and sex characteristics are not explicitly covered in anti-discrimination law — a visitor-specific impact is not documented.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Legal trajectory: the self-determination regime replaced a long, costly judicial procedure — a bill was presented in May 2017 and parliament approved the simplified civil-status change in July 2018. In July 2025 the government unveiled a comprehensive LGBTIQ+ action plan, criticised by local organisations for missing depathologisation and other elements. A 2019 report noted the law lacked LGBTphobic aggravating circumstances while the justice minister signalled evolution after a monitoring body's intervention.
rewrites.localsOnly: The self-determination legal-gender-recognition process (notably open to foreign nationals) is resident-facing administrative law. Civil-register amendment covers gender and first names; there is no nonbinary marker. An equality body and the national action plan serve residents' complaints and protections.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Nothing material remains unresolved. One 2018 report of the parliamentary vote was paywalled, so the vote split could not be verified from the page; and no independent incident series is documented, so the absence of recorded anti-trans violence rests on a thin cited record.

rewrites.summary:
Monaco is workable for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. Hate crimes and hate speech based on sexual orientation are penalised, and discrimination on grounds including gender identity is banned. A visitor faces no legal exposure whatsoever: no bathroom laws, no border friction (a tiny tourist enclave embedded in the neighbouring country of France, entry under the common border-free travel zone), no documented anti-trans incidents, and street violence of any kind is rare in this heavily-policed, very low-crime destination.

The score reflects the gap between de facto safety (very high) and legal thinness: no functioning legal gender recognition process and limited explicit trans protections.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Context and climate: regional LGBT-rights rankings place this nation near the bottom despite decriminalisation going back centuries; reporting notes only roughly ten people dare to be openly out; some travel guides describe a luxury/relaxation destination with an LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation directory but no discernible local scene — no Pride is held anywhere in it, so visitors are directed to the neighbouring country for one.
rewrites.localsOnly: The absence of any functioning legal-gender-recognition process is resident-facing: no administrative route exists for residents to amend a registered gender.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Family-law gaps (no marriage equality, cohabitation contracts only) are resident-facing concerns kept out of the visitor score, per the record's existing split. Very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty. One source notes reported discrimination is described as rare, but no independent verification of current practice exists in the record.

Travel guide page: no Pride is held anywhere in the destination (visitors are sent to a neighbouring country for one); pitched as a luxury/relaxation destination with an LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation directory but no discernible local scene.
Official human-rights report (2023): no significant changes; significant issues limited to libel and lèse-majesté laws (not enforced); no torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses reported.

News report (March 2025): decriminalisation going back centuries, yet the nation ranks near the bottom of regional LGBT-rights rankings — no equal succession, survivor pensions or parental leave for same-sex partners; roughly ten people openly out; a regional watchdog rapporteur called it a sad balance sheet.

rewrites.summary:
San Marino is workable for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. There is no functioning legal-gender-recognition process (a resident-facing gap only), no criminalisation, no bathroom law, no border friction (open border with the neighbouring country of Italy), and no documented pattern of anti-trans violence in this tiny, heavily tourism-dependent nation surrounded by Italy.

The score reflects very high de facto safety combined with minimal explicit legal infrastructure for trans people. For a visitor, no legal exposure is documented.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Legal trajectory: a 2018 law provided civil unions; a 2019 referendum inserted into the constitution a clause prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation; a 2022 appointment put an openly gay politician into the rotating six-month national-leadership role — reported as the first openly gay national leader anywhere — while the same report notes homosexuality was punishable by jail time until 2004 and recognition of gay couples followed in 2016; the 2019 periodic human-rights-review cycle recorded SOGIESC recommendations that the country accepted.
rewrites.localsOnly: No functioning legal-gender-recognition process — resident-facing gap: residents have no administrative route to amend a registered gender. No other resident-facing facts are recorded.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The legal-gender-recognition absence is resident-facing; no visitor exposure is documented. Very small population — the evidence base is thin, and this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty. No source addresses border-screening or document-practice for trans visitors, and no marriage- or partner-travel-specific rule or incident for visitors is recorded.

Liechtenstein is workable for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. Same-sex relations are legal and discrimination based on sexual orientation is banned, but gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics are not included in any anti-discrimination legislation, and there is no legal gender recognition law; these gaps are resident-facing, and a visitor faces no legal exposure.

No documented pattern of anti-trans violence, no bathroom law, no border friction (entry under the common border-free travel zone via its neighbours Switzerland and Austria), in a very small, very low-crime country closely integrated with those neighbours. Social attitudes are conservative but not mobilised-hostile. Marriage and joint adoption have been available since January 2025.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Context and flux: a September 2022 parliamentary motion sought to open civil marriage regardless of gender and sexual orientation and to remove all remaining legal differences, noting that registered partnerships were seen as a 'second-class marriage' and that the monarch said in 2021 he had nothing against marriage equality except adoption; earlier the same monarch called rainbow families 'irresponsible' in a New Year interview, remarks that local organisations and a political party said were contrary to the constitution and regional human-rights-law obligations. A 2016 press feature covered small nations 'playing catch-up' on equality, including this one.

rewrites.summary:
Vatican City is workable for trans visitors — an unusual case: a tiny 0.49 km² tourist enclave with essentially no resident jurisdiction a traveler can fall afoul of. Nothing about being trans is criminalised; there are no bathroom inspections, no morality police, and the guards and gendarmerie do not police tourist gender expression. Millions of tourists of every presentation visit annually without incident; entry is via the neighbouring city of Rome with no border formality.

The doctrinal climate is hostile — the 2024 declaration "Infinite Dignity" condemned gender-affirming surgery and "gender theory" as violations of human dignity, and no legal recognition or protection of any kind exists — but this is a climate signal, not a traveler-facing mechanism: the realistic worst case for a visitor is being refused entry to the basilica over a dress-code dispute (shoulders/knees rules apply to everyone).
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Doctrinal and diplomatic context: a 2008 episode saw the national government block a foreign government's first-choice ambassador because he is gay; an educational document (2019) opposes 'gender theory' as denying natural difference; a 2023 declaration permits spontaneous blessings for same-sex couples while forbidding any rite resembling marriage, with a January 2024 clarification reiterating that blessings never extend to the unions themselves; and the institutional posture against homosexuality drives policy in ways that remain distinct from the tiny nation's own law, which has recorded no modern criminal-law persecution of consensual conduct.
rewrites.localsOnly: No resident-facing record exists: no cultural-gender-role, birth-register or resident-discrimination fact is documented for this jurisdiction, and resident jurisdiction itself is essentially absent.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Doctrinal positions are climate signals, not enforcement mechanisms; the nation's employment and canon-law matters are resident-facing and excluded from the visitor score. Very small population — the evidence base is thin, and this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty. No source addresses document checks or screening for visitors beyond the recorded absence of border formality, and marriage/partner-travel questions for visitors are undocumented.
